scenes.purpose: Open on the low-inflation claim in the president's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only: the quoted words appear as spoken; "very little" holds and turns amber.

citations.label: Donald Trump, Kalispell, Montana rally, Oct 2026

scenes.direction: Cold open; the quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: At a rally in Montana this October, President Trump told the crowd, "we have very little inflation".

scenes.purpose: Set the opposite claim against it.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirroring sc01; "higher" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "inflation is higher than when he took office"

scenes.direction: Hard cut from sc01 so the two quotes read as a pair.
scenes.narration: On CBS News, a politics reporter put it the other way: "inflation is higher than when he took office".

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: The question types on, large and centred.
onScreenText: Very little, or more than before?

scenes.direction: Hold on the question through the second clause.
scenes.narration: Very little, or more than before? Let's put both claims against the government's own price index.

scenes.purpose: Give the boldest version of the claim.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "don't" holds and turns amber.

citations.label: Donald Trump, via Face the Nation

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; the quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: Start with the boldest version: Trump has also said, flatly, "we don't have inflation".

scenes.purpose: Answer the denial with the September CPI release.

visual.description: Two tiles: the 12-month rise lands first on "3.7 percent", the monthly rise second on "month to month".

chart.title: Consumer prices, September
chart.note: CPI-U; the monthly change is seasonally adjusted, the yearly change is not.

scenes.direction: Tiles count up as their figures are spoken.
scenes.narration: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' September report says otherwise: consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than a year earlier, and still rising month to month.

scenes.purpose: Turn the argument from whether to how high, and name the yardstick.

visual.description: One line, large: the yardstick question that runs through the video.

scenes.direction: Line appears on "compare it with"; brief hold.
scenes.narration: So there is inflation. The real argument is whether it's high, and that depends on what you compare it with.

scenes.purpose: Give the comparison with the past in the president's words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "worst" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "we inherited the worst inflation in history"

citations.label: Donald Trump, Kalispell, Montana rally, Oct 2026

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; the quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: Trump's comparison is the past: "we inherited the worst inflation in history", he told the Montana rally.

scenes.purpose: Show the 2022 peak against today's rate.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars: June 2022 grows long on "9.1 percent", September 2026 grows to less than half its length on "less than half".

chart.title: Consumer prices, change over 12 months
chart.note: CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted; this series cannot rank all of history.

scenes.direction: Second bar grows after the first settles.
scenes.narration: These figures can't rank all of history, but the 2022 peak was real: in June 2022 the yearly rate hit 9.1 percent, and today's is less than half of that.

scenes.purpose: Give the strongest version of the low-inflation case, from January.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "lowest" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "the lowest we've had in five years"

scenes.direction: Quote lands on the quoted words in the second half of the narration.
scenes.narration: And early this year, the low-inflation case was strong. Of January's reading, the YouTube channel The Right-Wing Populist said it was "the lowest we've had in five years".

scenes.purpose: Check the January claim: close to the low since 2021 and to pre-pandemic pace.

visual.description: Three short bars of nearly equal length: January 2026, the lowest reading since March 2021, and February 2020; the near-equality is the point.

scenes.direction: Bars grow one per clause.
scenes.narration: Close enough: the January rate was 2.4 percent, a whisker above the lowest reading since March 2021 and about the pace of early 2020 just before the pandemic.

scenes.purpose: Show September above every month of 2024 and 2025, and above what the administration inherited.

visual.description: Three bars: the highest month of 2024-2025 and September 2026 on s11, then January 2025 on s12, labelled as the month the administration took office.

scenes.direction: January 2025 bar grows on "3.0 percent"; hold after "CBS was making".
scenes.narration: By September, that case had gone: the yearly rate was higher than in any month of 2024 or 2025. It was also above the 3.0 percent of January 2025 (the month the administration took office): what he actually inherited, and the comparison CBS was making.

scenes.purpose: Give the shorter-window claim in the president's words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "1.7%" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "we're at 1.7% inflation for the last three months"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; the quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: Trump has a shorter window in mind: "we're at 1.7% inflation for the last three months", he told reporters.

scenes.purpose: Show the monthly changes behind both three-month windows.

visual.description: Four index-level tiles: May, June, August, September. On s15 June and September light as the window ends; on s16 the highlight slides back to May and August, and June turns red as the level that fell.

chart.title: Consumer price index level, seasonally adjusted
chart.note: Index levels; the annual paces in the narration are computed from them, not shown.

scenes.direction: Window highlight moves on "slide that window back".
scenes.narration: The index says otherwise: from June to September, the seasonally adjusted index ran at a pace of about 4.6 percent a year. To be fair, slide that window back one month, to end in August, and the pace drops to about 0.2 percent a year, because prices fell in June.

scenes.purpose: Land the lesson of the window.

visual.description: One line slams on, large.
onScreenText: Pick your window, pick your answer.

scenes.direction: Hold after the line.
scenes.narration: Pick your window, and you pick your answer.

scenes.purpose: Bring in the Fed's yardstick: its target.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "above target" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "for more than five years, inflation has been running above target"

scenes.direction: Quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: The Federal Reserve, for its part, said at its September press conference that "for more than five years, inflation has been running above target".

scenes.purpose: Set the Fed's goal beside its own 2026 projection.

visual.description: Two tiles: the 2 percent goal on "2 percent", then the officials' 2026 PCE projection on "3.7 percent", labelled PCE.

chart.title: The Fed's yardstick
chart.note: The projection is the median for the coming year, on PCE, not CPI.

citations.label: FOMC summary of economic projections, Sep 2026

scenes.direction: Second tile lands on "3.7 percent".
scenes.narration: Its stated goal is 2 percent, and its own officials expect 3.7 percent over 2026 on the price index they forecast, called PCE, short for personal consumption expenditures.

scenes.purpose: Show the CPI floor since 2021.

visual.description: One big tile: the lowest 12-month CPI rate in any month since March 2021.

chart.title: Lowest yearly CPI rate since March 2021
chart.note: CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted; October 2025 has no reading.

scenes.direction: Tile counts up on "2.3 percent".
scenes.narration: On the consumer price index, the yearly rate hasn't dropped below 2.3 percent in any month with a reading since March 2021.

scenes.purpose: Turn from the rate to the price level.

visual.description: The question types on, large and centred.
onScreenText: If the rate comes down, will prices?

scenes.direction: Typed on as spoken.
scenes.narration: And if the rate does come down, will prices?

scenes.purpose: Let the low-inflation channel make the point itself.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "expanding" and "decreasing" each turn amber as spoken.
onScreenText: "prices are technically expanding, but the actual rate is decreasing"

scenes.direction: Quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: Even The Right-Wing Populist says not: "prices are technically expanding, but the actual rate is decreasing".

scenes.purpose: Show the rate falling while the price level kept rising.

visual.description: Four tiles in two rows: the yearly rate falling from January 2023 to September 2024 on top, the index level rising over the same months beneath.

chart.title: January 2023 to September 2024
chart.note: CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted; the rise in the price level is computed from the index levels shown.

scenes.direction: Rate tiles on the first clause, index tiles on "the price level itself rose".
scenes.narration: That's what happened after the peak: from January 2023 to September 2024, the yearly rate fell from 6.4 percent to 2.4, while the price level itself rose about 5.4 percent.

scenes.purpose: Close the first question and open the second.

visual.description: Lines build one per clause: the two verdicts, then the next question.

scenes.direction: Hold on the question before the section turns.
scenes.narration: So inflation is not gone, and it is not at its peak. Which leaves the next question: what is pushing it up?

scenes.purpose: Show the spring climb.

visual.description: Four bars, February to May 2026, each growing on its figure; the last three climb.

scenes.direction: February is up first; March, April and May grow on their figures.
scenes.narration: The rate had been easing into the new year; then, from March to May, it climbed to 3.3, 3.8 and 4.2 percent.

scenes.purpose: Give the news explanation for the jump.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, two lines appearing as spoken; "Iran war" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "heading towards that number earlier this year"
"but then with the Iran war prices shot up"

scenes.direction: Each line lands on its phrase.
scenes.narration: NBC News said the economy had been "heading towards that number earlier this year", the Fed's target, "but then with the Iran war prices shot up".

scenes.purpose: Show gasoline's spring leap, and that the tables do not apportion it.

visual.description: Three tiles, March to May: gasoline monthly change; March lands large on "24.9 percent", April and May follow on "kept rising through May".

chart.title: Gasoline index, change over the month, 2026
chart.note: CPI-U gasoline, not seasonally adjusted; the tables do not say how much of the overall rise it explains.

scenes.direction: Tiles stay empty through s27; they fill from s41.
scenes.narration: The price tables confirm the jump, but they don't say what caused it. One line in them stands out, though: gasoline's own index leapt 24.9 percent in March alone and kept rising through May before falling back in June, but the tables don't say how much of the overall jump that explains.

scenes.purpose: Show September's report saying gasoline drove over half the month's rise.

visual.description: The release paragraph with the gasoline sentence highlighted as it is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: gasoline rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase

scenes.direction: Push in to the highlight.
scenes.narration: September's report is more specific: gasoline rose 9.1 percent in that one month and accounted for over half of the month's whole rise.

scenes.purpose: Give the economist's objection that it is not only fuel.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; the list of items appears as spoken.
onScreenText: "the war in Iran is not causing medical care, dental care, toys, apparel"

scenes.direction: Quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: But an economist on PBS NewsHour pointed out that "the war in Iran is not causing medical care, dental care, toys, apparel".

scenes.purpose: Show the report listing other items that rose.

visual.description: The release paragraph on core with the list of rising indexes highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care, and apparel

scenes.direction: Highlight sweeps along the list as it is read.
scenes.narration: The report agrees that it isn't only fuel: used cars, airline fares, medical care and apparel all went up in September.

scenes.purpose: Show that core was modest.

visual.description: Two tiles labelled core: the monthly rise on "0.3 percent", the yearly on "2.6 percent".

chart.title: Core prices (excluding food and energy), September

scenes.direction: Tiles count up on their figures.
scenes.narration: But the spread is modest: prices outside food and energy, called core, rose 0.3 percent on the month, no faster than in August, and 2.6 percent over the year.

scenes.purpose: Give the case that underlying inflation is higher.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "around 3%" holds and turns amber.

scenes.direction: Quote lands on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: Some economists think the underlying rate is higher. "I think underlying inflation is around 3%", Michael Strain said in June.

scenes.purpose: Set core's range and shelter against Strain's figure.

visual.description: Horizontal bars: core's lowest and highest months of 2026 and its summer 2025 rate on s33, then shelter on s34, the longest of the 2026 bars.

scenes.direction: Shelter bar grows on "Housing runs hotter".
scenes.narration: Core has run a little under that all year, between 2.4 and 2.9 percent, and it had slowed from 3.1 percent in the summer of 2025 before ticking back up. Housing runs hotter: the shelter index rose 3.2 percent over the year.

scenes.purpose: Give the New York Fed's tariff estimate.

visual.description: One big tile: the estimated cumulative tariff effect on the goods studied, by February 2026.

chart.title: Tariffs and the goods studied

points.label: Added to price growth by February 2026

chart.note: Percentage points, for the goods in the study's sample only; relative to less-exposed goods.

citations.label: NY Fed tariff pass-through study (Amiti, Heise, Weinstein)

scenes.direction: Tile counts up on "2.9 percentage points".
scenes.narration: And tariffs? Economists at the New York Fed estimate they added around 2.9 percentage points to price growth for the goods they studied, by February 2026.

scenes.purpose: Show the authors' own caution.

visual.description: The paper's paragraph with the caution highlighted.

citations.label: NY Fed tariff pass-through study (Amiti, Heise, Weinstein)

scenes.direction: Push in to the highlight on "illustrative".
scenes.narration: They caution that it measures those goods against less-exposed ones, so the number is illustrative, and it doesn't tell us how much of overall inflation tariffs explain.

scenes.purpose: Sum up the second question.

visual.description: Three lines build one per clause.

scenes.direction: Hold on the full list.
scenes.narration: So in September the biggest single push was gasoline, while core sat a little under Strain's figure, with housing above it.

scenes.purpose: Name what the argument was really about.

visual.description: One line, large.

scenes.direction: Line appears on "yardstick".
scenes.narration: The people quoted here mostly weren't arguing about the numbers; they were arguing about the yardstick.

scenes.purpose: Give the viewer the two questions to ask.

visual.description: Two lines build as spoken.

scenes.direction: Each line on its phrase.
scenes.narration: So when someone tells you inflation is high or low, ask: compared with what, and over which months?

scenes.purpose: Leave the viewer with the rate-versus-prices point.

visual.description: Two lines build as spoken.
onScreenText: A slower rate still means climbing prices

scenes.direction: Hold on the last line; fade out.
scenes.narration: And when you hear the rate is falling, check core, and remember that a slower rate still means prices that are climbing.
